source.title: Open Questions in Cosmic-Ray Research at Ultrahigh Energies

accepted.question_text: Which astrophysical source populations produce the bulk of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays, understood as cosmic rays with energies above 10^18 eV, and can any candidate class simultaneously satisfy the requirements for acceleration to about 10^20 eV, enough total energy production to explain the observed diffuse flux, sufficient local source density to avoid excessive small-scale clustering, and compatibility with the observed mass composition?

evidence.quote: Cosmic rays with energy exceeding 1018 eV≡ 1 EeV, are referred to as ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs).

Nevertheless, many aspects of the nature of UHECRs remain an enigma: What is the origin of these particles? What is their mass composition? How do the astrophysical sources accelerate particles to such extreme energies?

The challenge of accelerating cosmic rays to1020 eV was succinctly presented in the form of the minimum requirement for the accelerators, in what is now commonly referred to as the “Hillas condition” [ 125].
Another condition that must be met by UHECR accelerators is that they must possess the required energy budget to produce the observed UHECR diffuse ﬂux.

The lack of signiﬁcant clustering in the arrival directions of UHECRs with energy exceeding 70 EeV was used to derive a lower limit to the UHECR source number density, considering that UHECRs might have suffered deﬂections as large as 30◦.

accepted.question_text: Above roughly 10^19.4 eV, are the differences between the ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray energy spectra measured by the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array caused by experiment-specific systematic effects in energy reconstruction and calibration, or by astrophysical differences because the observatories view different parts of the sky?

evidence.quote: However, above this energy, larger differences remain present, which cannot be accounted for by an independent scaling of their reconstructed energies.

It will be important to understand whether this difference is caused by systematic uncertainties arising at the highest energies only, or whether it has an astrophysics origin related to seeing different parts of the sky.
As it is still too early to draw deﬁnite conclusions about the source of the differences, the joint working group will continue their studies.

accepted.question_text: What causes the suppression, or cut-off, of the cosmic-ray flux at the highest observed energies: energy losses during propagation such as the Greisen-Zatsepin-Kuzmin effect on cosmic background photons, a maximum acceleration energy imposed by nearby sources, or a combination of propagation effects and source-limited maximum energy?
accepted.context_brief: Origin of the highest-energy flux suppression

evidence.quote: Another important question related to the UHECR energy spectrum is about the origin of the ﬂux suppression observed at the highest energies.
The cut-off at the highest energies in the cosmic-ray spectrum has been established unambiguously recently, but the origin of this most prominent and signiﬁcant feature is still a matter of debate.
The results question the interpretation of the ﬂux suppression as caused solely by the GZK effect.
In such a scenario, the ﬂux suppression is a combination of propagation effects and the maximum energy at the source.

accepted.question_text: What is the mass composition of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays at the highest energies, especially around and above 10^20 eV, and does the observed trend toward heavier primaries near ultrahigh energies continue, flatten, or change when larger statistics and better hadronic-interaction modeling become available?

evidence.quote: Nevertheless, many aspects of the nature of UHECRs remain an enigma: What is the origin of these particles? What is their mass composition? How do the astrophysical sources accelerate particles to such extreme energies?
As of today, no composition fractions are available around and above 1020 eV.

These measurements of the ﬁrst two moments (mean and standard deviation) of theXmax distribution suggest that the composition of cosmic rays becomes lighter as the energy increases towards the ankle (until around 1018.3 eV) and then becomes heavier again when approaching ultrahigh energies.
Due to the limited statistics and unknowns about hadronic interaction models, this trend is still largely uncertain.

accepted.question_text: Is the observed energy-dependent sequence of ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray mass groups caused by a Peters cycle in which the maximum source energy scales with rigidity E/Z, by photonuclear spallation during propagation to Earth or inside the source so that the relevant scale is energy per nucleon E/A, or by a combination of these mechanisms, and what observations would disentangle them?

evidence.quote: The sequence of alternating groups of elements and the increase of mass with energy could be caused by a Peters cycle [120] at the accelerators, i.e., maximum energy that depends on rigidity R = E/Z or due to photonuclear spallation processes during propagation (e.g. [121–123]) to Earth and in the source [124], leading to scaling with energy per nucleon E/A.
The factor between the maximum fraction of protons and helium in Figure 5 is close to 4, which would favor a spallation scenario.

Only the detection of several cycles (if any) will allow for an unambiguous disentanglement of the combined effect of spallation effects from the propagation to Earth and the possible existence of a Peters cycle and/or photonuclear interactions in the source.

accepted.question_text: How does the average rigidity R = E/Z of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays evolve with energy, and does that evolution make magnetic deflections small enough at the highest energies for anisotropy and source-correlation studies, despite the simultaneous trend toward heavier average mass?

evidence.quote: Another important open question related to mass composition is the evolution of the rigidity R = E/Z with energy.

As can be seen, the rigidity is increasing with energy and therefore the angular deﬂection in magnetic ﬁelds should decrease with energy, i.e., the increase in the average mass of cosmic rays with energy as shown in ﬁgure 5 is slow enough to not outrun the increase of energy.
No high-quality data currently exists at ultrahigh energies where hints for anisotropies at intermediate scales were reported.

accepted.question_text: Which galaxies or galaxy types host ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray accelerators above the ankle, and what combination of full-sky exposure, redshift-evolution constraints, complete source catalogs, and joint energy-composition-arrival-direction analyses is needed to turn statistical correlations with catalogs into credible source identification rather than spurious correlation?

evidence.quote: Most likely, not all galaxies behave as UHE accelerators, so that the question of which galaxies or galaxy types host UHE accelerators remains open.
Even if such an anisotropic signal reached the 5σ discovery threshold in the near future, it probably would not be sufﬁcient to claim identiﬁcation of UHECR sources.

Such a feat would require coverage over the entire celestial sphere — to avoid blind regions where a different source type could contribute — constraints on the redshift evolution of the UHECR production rate — to enable a tomographic probe of source populations — and completeness in the source models up to the propagation horizon and down to a sufﬁciently low luminosity.
These recent works suggest the possibility in the mid-term future to design analyses jointly accounting for the energy, composition, and arrival directions of UHECRs.

accepted.question_text: What event-by-event energy resolution, mass resolution, and total exposure are needed for future ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray observatories to identify individual sources while limiting spillover from lower-energy isotropic events and limiting the blurring produced by heavier, more strongly deflected primaries?
accepted.context_brief: Resolution and exposure for source searches

evidence.quote: Identifying individual sources of UHECR would answer that question and remains the ultimate goal of future studies.

Identifying such sources calls for a precise shower-by-shower determination of the energy and mass of the primary particle to avoid cosmic rays of lower energy diluting the event sample and to avoid heavy primaries, suffering stronger deﬂections, blurring the source spots in the sky.

Assuming all events belowEthresh being isotropic and those above being correlated to sources, 58 % of the events observed above the applied threshold would be isotropic background and dilute the signal.
However, the ﬂux of UHECRs drops at the same time by an increase of a factor of two, so that the relaxation in energy resolution from 10 % to 30 % needs to be compensated by a factor two in exposure.

accepted.question_text: What physical acceleration mechanisms can accelerate cosmic rays beyond PeV energies and up to ultrahigh energies near 10^20 eV under realistic source conditions, rather than merely satisfying the Hillas confinement condition, and how can these mechanisms be studied under conditions as close as possible to those in real astrophysical sources?

evidence.quote: How do the astrophysical sources accelerate particles to such extreme energies?

It states that a necessary condition to accelerate particles to ultrahigh energy is that of conﬁnement; particles can stay in the acceleration region as long as their Larmor radius is smaller than the size of the accelerator.

The conﬁnement condition is not sufﬁcient to guarantee cosmic-ray acceleration to1020 eV . This depends on the details of the acceleration mechanism and the timescale for energy loss in the source environment.

Action item 5: Perform detailed studies of particle acceleration in collisionless shocks and magnetic reconnection under conditions as close to those in real sources, either via simulations or in the lab, when possible.

accepted.question_text: What is the physical origin of the knee, second-knee or iron-knee, and ankle features in the cosmic-ray spectrum between about 10^15 and 10^18 eV, and at which feature does the transition from Galactic cosmic rays to an extragalactic component begin? In particular, are the knee features produced by propagation changes, by maximum energies of Galactic sources such as supernova remnants, or by another mechanism?

evidence.quote: The cosmic-ray spectrum features three distinct spectral breaks in the energy range between1015−1018eV. In order of increasing energy, these are the “knee”, “second-knee” (or “iron-knee”) , and “ankle”, illustrated in Figure 12.
The physical origin of the knee feature remains unclear. Both a propagation and sources maximum energy origin of this feature remain viable candidates.
However, whether SNRs are actually able to accelerate up to the knee energy (3 PeV) remains an open question.
If the interpretation of these observational results is correct, the onset of this new light component marks the beginning of an extragalactic component in the arriving CR ﬂux.

accepted.question_text: For each candidate source class of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays, over which energy ranges should the observed flux be modeled as steady and over which ranges should it be modeled as transient, given the ratio of propagation time to source emission time, magnetic-horizon effects, and energy losses? For gamma-ray bursts in particular, can they operate as efficient accelerators on the required timescales and remain viable ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray sources?

evidence.quote: For UHECR sources, what deﬁnes whether a candidate object is classiﬁed as a transient or steady source is the ratio of the mean propagation timescale between sources to the source emission timescale, tprop/temiss.
These results leave unclear whether GRBs operate as efﬁcient particle accelerators (i.e. close to the Bohm limit), and on what timescale the acceleration takes place on.
It therefore remains unclear whether these objects can be considered as viable UHECR sources.
Indeed, it is possible for a source class to only achieve steady-state emission in a ﬁnite energy range, both below and above which the cosmic-ray ﬂux is only transient.

accepted.question_text: What are the strength, structure, and local-universe distribution of Galactic and extragalactic magnetic fields, and how do these fields deflect and time-delay ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays strongly enough to affect spectrum, composition, anisotropy, and the feasibility of charged-particle astronomy?

evidence.quote: Magnetic ﬁelds in scales comparable to and larger than the size of the Galaxy may affect the propagation of UHECRs.
Little is known about extragalactic magnetic ﬁelds (EGMFs).
Ultimately the deﬂection of UHECRs in EGMFs depends on the distribution of EGMFs in the local Universe.

Given the considerable uncertainties in the GMF and the inconclusive results on the effects of EGMFs on cosmic-ray propagation due to the model dependencies, the unambiguous identiﬁcation of individual UHECRs will require better constraints on EGMFs and improved models of the GMF.

accepted.question_text: Why do extensive air-shower measurements at very high energies contain roughly 30-60% more muons than current hadronic-interaction models predict, and can the muon excess be explained by conventional improvements to Standard Model hadronic generators, or does it point to physics beyond the Standard Model?

evidence.quote: Depending on the interaction model used for reference and the measurement, there are about30−60% more muons found in data than predicted.

This muon puzzle is one of the most important problems in hadronic interaction physics as it is very difﬁcult, if not impossible, to increase the number of muons by such a large fraction just by changing the physics of the ﬁrst interaction.
First of all, there is the muon discrepancy that is still not understood.

Conventional explanations of the muon discrepancy have to be developed to ﬁnd out whether we indeed have to assume that the muon excess is related to physics beyond the Standard Model of particle physics.

accepted.question_text: Which accelerator, fixed-target, forward-physics, and air-shower measurements are needed to improve hadronic-interaction models enough to reduce systematic uncertainties in ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray mass-composition inference, especially for pion-proton, kaon-proton, pion-light-nuclei, kaon-light-nuclei, proton-oxygen, and forward secondary-particle production?

evidence.quote: An important aspect of the hadronic interaction models is the extrapolation of accelerator data to center-of-mass energies of up to √s ∼ 400 TeV , well beyond energies accessible at colliders, to forward phase space regions not accessible in experiments, and to projectile and target particle combinations not measured in accelerator experiments.
Additional data from collider and ﬁxed-target experiments and progress in the theory and phenomenology of multiparticle production are required to lower these uncertainties.
Of prime importance are the measurement of the pion-proton, kaon-proton, pion-light-nuclei, and kaon-light-nuclei cross sections and the corresponding distributions of leading secondary particles.
Taking data of proton-oxygen at LHC is technically possible and would be a key measurement for improving air shower predictions.
Closely related to this transition between two regimes is the question of non-linear effects, or even parton density saturation, expected at very high parton densities.

accepted.question_text: Can ultrahigh-energy cosmic-ray propagation and air-shower development reveal Lorentz-invariance violation or other new high-energy physics, and what observable signatures, such as vacuum Cherenkov energy losses, modified interaction thresholds, suppressed neutral-pion production, or sharp changes in muon number, would distinguish such effects from conventional hadronic-model shortcomings?

evidence.quote: Thus, UHECR propagation in the cosmic radiation backgrounds, which have energyϵ≪ GeV , cannot probe Lorentz-invariant physics beyond the Standard Model, but it can still probe invariance violations under Lorentz boosts.

In addition, the development of air showers can be inﬂuenced both by Lorentz-invariant new physics acting on primaries or secondaries with energy E ≳ 2× 1017 eV and targets of mass ϵ ≳ mN, and also by Lorentz-invariance violations involving large Lorentz boosts.
One could imagine such effects to have energy thresholds, so one could also search for comparatively large increases of muon number over a small primary energy range.

Therefore, assuming neutral pions still decay quasi-instantaneously, the most likely explanation of the observed large muon number is a signiﬁcant decrease in the fraction of energy going into neutral pions, fπ0.
Therefore, observing a particle of energy E implies Ecr ≳ E which, from Eq. (8), leads to an upper bound on η.

accepted.question_text: What fluxes of cosmogenic neutrinos and gamma rays, produced when ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays interact with extragalactic background photons during propagation, should be expected across the allowed source-composition, maximum-energy, source-evolution, magnetic-field, and hadronic-model parameter space, and what would those neutral secondary messengers reveal about the sources of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays?

evidence.quote: Neutral secondaries including neutrinos and photons are expected to be produced when UHECRs interact with extragalactic background photons during intergalactic propagation.
Their ﬂux mainly depends on the chemical composition, maximum energy of UHECRs, and the source evolution model (e.g., [61, 62]; see [63, 64] for secondaries from heavy nuclei).
What is the ﬂux of secondary messengers — neutrinos, gamma rays — associated with UHECRs, and what can we infer from them about UHECR sources?

Action item 7: Generate predictions of the cosmogenic neutrino ﬂux by scanning across all of the available parameter space of UHECR model parameters — including uncertainties in magnetic ﬁelds and hadronic interaction models — in order to fully characterize the uncertainties.

accepted.question_text: How can future detections of EeV-energy cosmogenic or point-source neutrinos be used to test neutrino-nucleon cross sections, neutrino flavor composition, Lorentz-violation-like effects, neutrino decay, equivalence-principle violation, or other new physics over gigaparsec baselines, while separating fundamental effects from astrophysical uncertainties in spectra, source evolution, arrival directions, and flavor identification?

evidence.quote: Cosmogenic neutrinos, with EeV energies, when discovered, could extend the reach of these tests.

Cosmogenic neutrinos could be used to measure the cross section at the EeV scale for the ﬁrst time, test strong dynamics more deeply than colliders [351, 352], and search for new physics at an even higher energy scale.

New physics of different types can affect all neutrino observables: the energy spectrum (see, e.g., [368–374]), distribution of arrival directions (see,e.g., [375, 376]), and the ﬂavor composition, i.e., the proportion of each neutrino ﬂavor to the total in the incoming ﬂux (see, e.g., [377–380]).

Numerous new-physics models have effects that are proportional to some power of the neutrino energyE and to the propagated distance L, i.e., they grow as∼ κnEnL, where the energy dependence n and the proportionality constant κn are model-dependent.

For instance, for neutrino decay [353–355], n =−1; for CPT-odd Lorentz violation [356–358] or coupling to a torsion ﬁeld [359], n = 0; and for CPT-even Lorentz violation [360, 361] or violation of the equivalence principle [362–365], n = 1.

When extracting fundamental neutrino properties from the data, one must factor in astrophysical uncertainties (e.g., shape of the energy spectrum, redshift evolution of the number density of sources, etc.), which can be signiﬁcant;
Action item 8: Generate updated predictions of the emission of UHE neutrinos from point sources, steady-state and transient.
